overview: Tlingit homelands include coastal and inland communities connected through clans, trade and language. This broad imported coastal outline is not a single kingdom or a precise boundary. The examples here identify particular communities, especially the Kiks.ádi at Sitka and Huna Tlingit at Glacier Bay.

periods.title: Clans and coastal resources
periods.summary: Families maintained relationships with particular places, foods and ancestral histories.

periods.title: Trade and resistance
periods.summary: Russian colonial expansion brought violent conflict at Sitka, followed by continuing Tlingit resistance and negotiation.

periods.title: Continuing communities
periods.summary: The United States claimed Alaska, while Tlingit communities continued their own histories and institutions.

items.text: At Glacier Bay, clan histories connect particular places to ancestors, songs, crests and responsibilities. Gathering foods such as salmon, halibut, berries and gull eggs also maintains relationships with the homeland. A place that a visitor calls wilderness can be a deeply familiar family landscape.

Sitka Kiks.ádi families moved from winter villages to salmon-stream camps in summer. Some camp houses used bark or boards brought from winter houses; structures could serve as both dwellings and smokehouses. Seasonal moving could involve taking parts of the house along.

Elder Herbert Hope supplied a map of remembered fishing structures in 1993. Archaeologists later found a salmon gaff, woodworking tools and hand-forged nails near a depression. These finds supported the identification of a smokehouse location remembered through family knowledge.

Food storage was part of preparing for difficult seasons. At the Sitka site, archaeologists investigated depressions interpreted as possible food caches; a tree growing into one showed that the pit was already there around 1830. The interpretation combines the ground’s shape, artifacts and tree growth.

Traditional wooden halibut hooks used a carefully shaped frame and barb. Sealaska Heritage explains that their proportions targeted medium-sized halibut while tending to spare very small and very large fish. The design depended on knowing how a halibut sucks food into its mouth.

Tlingit artist Héendei Donald Gregory taught hook-making in a 21-part video series released in 2021. Lessons include preparing, naming and baiting hooks. A useful fishing tool can carry artistic and spiritual knowledge as well as instructions for getting dinner onto the line.

Before the 1804 Russian attack, defenders built Shís’gi Noow beside shallow tidelands. The shallows kept heavily armed ships farther from the walls. Choosing the ground was part of the defense: geography could reduce an enemy’s advantage in cannon.

The defenders repelled the first Russian landing, but the loss of reserve gunpowder made continued defense difficult. The Kiks.ádi withdrew on the Survival March. Families abandoned houses and possessions to preserve their community and continue resistance from another position.

Withdrawal did not mean immediate submission. The Kiks.ádi blocked trade bound for Russian Sitka and dealt with American traders instead. In the early 1820s they rebuilt homes beside the Russian settlement, creating an uneasy neighborhood of trade, negotiation and competing claims.

The 2009 Dictionary of Tlingit records “Gunalchéesh!” with the translation “Thank you!” This is an attested modern written sample, with its spelling and accent marks preserved. It should not be mistaken for an inscription left at the 1804 fort.

The dictionary credits fluent speakers Anita Lafferty, John Marks, June Pegues and Helen Sarabia as its main language consultants. Preserving a language means listening carefully to knowledgeable people, including their examples, humor and differences in regional speech.

The Huna Ancestors’ House at Bartlett Cove opened on 25 August 2016 after years of collaboration between the Hoonah Indian Association and the National Park Service. Carved screens and posts accompany a place for community gatherings, teaching and renewed connections with Glacier Bay.

ending.text: The Russian settlement at Sitka and the 1867 transfer of Alaska did not end Tlingit people or their clan relationships. The modern Huna Tribal House is one example of continued cultural authority and community teaching. The map’s 1500 endpoint has no meaning as a national collapse.
